item.title: Query Complexity of Densest Sub(hyper)graph Problems
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Sinan G. Aksoy, Eli Friedman, Nate Veldt, Stephen J. Young

Rubinstein et al. introduce the study of connectivity and minimum cut problems in the cut query model, where an algorithm can only access the edges of a graph through CUT queries. In this work, we examine the query complexity of densest subgraph problems. Our first contribution is to generalize the uniform sparsification approach for Densest Subgraph and other heavy subgraph problems to weighted graphs, achieving the following results. >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Densest Subgraph in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, roughly matching the $Ω(n/\log n)$ lower bound we prove for randomized algorithms. >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Max Cut in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. This improves upon the bound of $O(n\log^3 n(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2))$ queries achieved by Plevrakis et al., making significant progress towards their lower bound of $Ω(n/\log n)$ queries. In contrast, we rule out approximation schemes with truly subquadratic query complexity for Densest $k$-Subgraph and settle its exact query complexity in both the unweighted and deterministic settings. For hypergraphs, we show CUT queries alone cannot achieve $o(\sqrt{n})$-approximation for Densest Subhypergraph or $o(n)$-approximation for Densest $k$-Subhypergraph, regardless of the number of queries. Augmenting CUT queries with the EDGE oracle of Chen et al., we overcome this barrier for Densest Subhypergraph and obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation on rank-$r$ hypergraphs using $O(nr\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We also extend our Densest $k$-Subgraph hardness results to hypergraphs and prove exponential query lower bounds for exact Densest $k$-Subhypergraph. Lastly, confirming a conjecture of Chakrabarty and Liao, we show that simulating an ADD query using CUT and IS-EDGE$^?$ queries requires exponentially-many queries.

item.title: Bipartite Matching with Few Rounds of Demand Queries
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Shravan Mehra, Sagnik Mukhopadhyay, Vihan Shah

We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items). For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+δ}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). Conversely, we give a randomised algorithm achieving approximation factor O(n^{(1-k*delta)/(k+1)}/k) in expectation. For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). Our algorithms produce matching and vertex-cover certificates; the deterministic trade-off also extends to minimum vertex cover and maximum fractional matching. We extend the randomised upper bounds to the weaker Demand-OR model [Nisan 2021]. We prove a non-adaptive simulation of uniform random-neighbour queries using known techniques, avoiding the O(log n)-round penalty of the trivial binary-search simulation. Consequently, our upper bounds yield the same k-round approximation guarantees using O(q * log^2 n) Demand-OR queries per round.

item.title: Path Length Existence Problems in Bounded-Treewidth Probabilistic Graphs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Antoine Amarilli, Mikaël Monet, Harshul Sagar

We consider the problem of computing the probability of existence of a source-to-target path or walk satisfying a given length constraint in an input probabilistic graph. The length constraints we consider can require the length to be at least $\ell$, at most $\ell$, or exactly $\ell$, for $\ell$ a target length given as input. The probabilistic graphs that we consider are directed graphs where each edge is annotated with an independent probability of existence. As this task is generally intractable (#P-hard), we aim for algorithms applying to input graphs that are assumed to be of bounded treewidth. We classify the complexity landscape of these problems: - We give an XP algorithm parameterised by treewidth to compute the probability that an input probabilistic graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length $\geq \ell$, and do the same for a path/walk of length $\leq \ell$. - We show that the four problems mentioned in the last item are W[1]-hard parameterised by pathwidth (hence not FPT under the standard assumption that FPT$\neq$W[1]). This is in contrast to the case of non-probabilistic graphs, where the corresponding problems were known to be FPT parameterised by treewidth; and to the connectivity problem (and more generally MSO evaluation) on probabilistic graphs, where the same was known. - Surprisingly, we show that it is #P-hard to compute the probability that an input graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length exactly $\ell$, even on graphs of pathwidth $2$. By contrast, all our problems are tractable on graphs of treewidth $1$. - Last, we investigate the complexity of our problems when the edges can carry weights. This causes all our problems to become #P-hard already on pathwidth-2 graphs, and causes specifically the ``exactly $\ell$'' walk problem to be #P-hard even on pathwidth-1 graphs.

item.title:
TR26-254 | Parameterized Uniformity Testing in the Huge Object Model |
Clément Canonne,
Sayantan Sen,
Joy Qiping Yang
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

We continue the study of distribution testing in the Huge Object Model (Goldreich and Ron, 2023), focusing on the flagship question of \emph{parameterized uniformity testing}: given access to data in $\{0,1\}^n$, is its underlying probability distribution uniform on a small subset of size $m$? The focus here is on both the number of data points required (sample complexity) and the number of bits from these data points one needs to observe (query complexity). While previous work fully characterized both of these in the ``tiny support'' regime $m \ll n$, very little was understood in the ``medium-to-large'' support one ($n \leq m \ll 2^n$). Our work remedies this state of affairs, establishing the existence of a sample-query complexity tradeoff and showing that (in contrast to the tiny-support regime) adaptive algorithms can significantly outperform non-adaptive ones.

item.title: Tree Edit Distance: Near-Linear-Time Approximate, Sublinear, and Dynamic
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Bingbing Hu, Tomasz Kociumaka, Jakob Nogler, Barna Saha

Tree edit distance (TED), the analog of string edit distance (ED) for hierarchical data, is the minimum number of node insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one labeled rooted ordered tree into another. We narrow polynomial gaps between TED and ED in near-linear-time approximation, sublinear algorithms, and dynamic algorithms. We give an $n^{o(1)}$-approximation in $O(n)$ time and, for every $0<δ<1$, a $(\log n)^{O(1/δ)}$-approximation in $O(n^{1+δ})$ time. This improves the previous near-linear-time $O(\sqrt n)$-approximation [Boroujeni et al., STOC'19] and brings TED to parity with ED in this regime up to polylogarithmic factors. With query access to the balanced-parentheses (Euler-tour) representation of the input trees, we give the first sublinear-time TED algorithm: for every $τ\in[1,n]$, it computes a $τn^{o(1)}$-approximation of $1+\mathrm{ted}$ in $O(n/τ)$ time. For dynamic TED, we give an exact algorithm with amortized update time $\tilde{O}(k^7)$ and a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation with amortized update time $\tilde{O}_{\varepsilon}(k)$, where $k$ caps the distance that must be reported. The exact algorithm is the first to beat recomputation in a nontrivial parameter regime. The approximation improves prior dynamic guarantees [Das et al., FOCS'25] and cannot be significantly improved in any parameter regime without a breakthrough for static $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of ED. All results use dynamic programming on a new hierarchical tree decomposition, analogous to partitioning strings into blocks of geometrically decreasing sizes. It combines structural properties previously achieved only in isolation, providing a framework for transferring algorithmic ideas from ED to TED, with additional ingredients addressing the obstacles in each computational setting.

item.title: Tolerant Testers for Subgraph-Freeness
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Reut Levi, Jonathan Meiri

In this paper we study the problem of tolerantly testing the property of being $H$-free (which also implies distance approximation from being $H$-free). In the general-graphs model, we show that tolerant $K_k$-freeness testing can be achieved with query complexity that is polynomial in the arboricity of the input graph $G$, $arb(G)$, and independent of the size of $G$ (for graphs in which the average degree is $Ω(1))$. Specifically for triangles, our algorithm distinguishes graphs which are $ε$-close to being triangle-free from graphs that are $3ε(1+η)$-far from being triangle-free with expected query complexity which is $\tilde{O}(arb^3(G))$ (for constant $η$ and $ε$). For general $k$-cliques our algorithm distinguishes graphs which are $ε$-close to being $K_k$-free from graphs which are ${k \choose 2}ε(1+η)$-far from being $K_k$-free with expected query complexity which is polynomial in $k$, $1/ε$, $1/η$ and $arb(G)$. We then generalize our result and provide a similar result for any motif $H$ which is $2$-connected and has radius $1$. This includes for example the wheel graph. Finally, we show that our tester can be applied to the bounded-degree model for tolerantly testing $H$-freeness for any motif $H$. The query complexity of the algorithm is polynomial in the degree bound, $d$, improving the previous state-of-the-art by Marko and Ron (TALG 2009) that obtained quasi-polynomial query complexity in $d$.

item.title: Testing Connectedness and Edge Connectedness
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Diptaksho Palit, Ramesh Krishnan S. Pallavoor, Sofya Raskhodnikova, Nithin Varma

We revisit the classical problem of testing connectedness of graphs represented in the adjacency lists model and obtain optimal bounds. Specifically, we show that $\varepsilon$-testing connectedness of graphs with maximum degree at most $d$ requires $Ω(\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon d})$ queries (when $\varepsilon \le \frac{1}{4d^5}$). Our result implies that the connectedness tester of Levi, Pallavoor, Raskhodnikova, and Varma ({\em ACM Trans.\ Comput.\ Theory, 2022}) is optimal. We also study the problem of testing $k$-edge-connectedness of both directed and undirected graphs of average degree $\overline{d}$ in the adjacency lists model and design a tester with query complexity $O(\frac{k}{\varepsilon} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon \overline{d}})$, improving upon the bounds by Forster, Nanongkai, Saranurak, Yang, and Yingchareonthawornchai (SODA 2020). Furthermore, we complement our upper bound by showing that every one-sided error $k$-edge-connectedness tester must make $Ω(k/\varepsilon)$ queries.

item.title: Incremental Exact Vertex Connectivity
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Felix Adena, Monika Henzinger, Christoph Kern, Daniel Rutschmann

We study the problem of maintaining the vertex connectivity $κ$ of a graph under edge insertions. For undirected graphs, our algorithm uses $O(κ^4 \log^2 n)$ amortized time per edge insertion. After each edge insertion, the algorithm outputs the current value of $κ$, plus a set of $κ$ vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. Our algorithm is Monte-Carlo randomized and works with a randomness-adaptive adversary. The algorithm also works on directed graphs against an oblivious adversary, which is equivalent to an output-adaptive adversary if we only have to output the current value of $κ$. Previously, algorithms for maintaining the vertex connectivity with $o(n)$ time per edge insertion were only known for $κ\le 2$, and need $\tilde{O}(\log^2 n)$ and $O(\sqrt{n})$ time per edge insertion for $κ= 1,2$, respectively. Moreover, for $κ> 4$, no algorithm faster than recomputation from scratch was known. We complement our algorithm with a conditional lower bound: Under the OMv conjecture, any insertions-only algorithm that outputs the current value of $κ$ after every insertion needs $Ω(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized time per edge insertion for $κ= Θ(n)$. Previous conditional lower bounds for this problem only apply to worst case running time, or algorithms that support both edge insertions and edge deletions.

item.title: The Six-Dimensional Tarski Problem is $Ω(\log^3 n)$-Hard
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Kristóf Zólomy

We study the deterministic query complexity of finding a fixed point of a monotone function $f:[n]^d\to[n]^d$, where querying $x$ returns $f(x)$. For fixed $d\ge2$, earlier work established a lower bound of $Ω((\log n)^2)$ and an upper bound of $O_d((\log n)^{\lceil(d+2)/3\rceil})$ for the query complexity. Very recently, several papers obtained improved lower bounds using AI-assisted proofs. In this paper, we further improve these lower bounds to $\text{Tarski}(n,d)=Ω_d((\log n)^{2+\lfloor\log_3(d/2)\rfloor})$. In particular, we obtain the optimal $Θ((\log n)^3)$ deterministic query complexity in six dimensions.

item.title: Improved Pass Complexity for Semi-Streaming Matching in General Graphs via Budgeted Price Approach
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Authors: Tatsuya Terao

We present a simple deterministic semi-streaming algorithm that computes a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum matching in general graphs in $O(1/\varepsilon^{2})$ passes. This matches the pass complexity of the auction algorithm of Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan~[SOSA'21] for bipartite graphs, and answers Open Question~2 of Assadi~[SOSA'24 \& TheoretiCS'25]. Our approach, which we call the \emph{budgeted price approach}, is very different from the previous $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$-pass semi-streaming algorithms for $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of matching in general graphs and improves their pass complexity. All previous approaches are augmenting-path-based and use $O(1/\varepsilon^{19})$ passes by Fischer, Mitrović, and Uitto~[STOC'22], $O(1/\varepsilon^{6})$ passes by Mitrović, Mukherjee, Sankowski, and Sheu~[ICALP'25], and $O(1/\varepsilon^{4})$ passes by Izumi, Kitamura, and Yamaguchi~['25].

item.title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: minimum cut

Authors: Ivan Fomin, Ivan Koryabkin, Boris Sheludko

Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.

item.title: Deterministic Global Minimum Cut Using $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ Cut Queries
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: minimum cut

Authors: Yotam Kenneth-Mordoch

Finding a global minimum cut in an unweighted graph is a fundamental task in the cut-query model. While there exists a randomized algorithm for this task using $\tilde O(n)$ queries, known deterministic algorithms use $\tilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ queries. We improve upon this result and give a simple deterministic algorithm that finds a global minimum cut using $\tilde O(\min\left\{ nδ,n^2/δ\right\})$ cut queries, which equals $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ in the worst case, where $δ$ is the minimum degree of the graph. The key ingredient in our approach is an efficient maximum $s,t$-flow algorithm, for the case when the minimum $s,t$-cut has value at most $δ$.

item.title: Online Graph Coloring with Random Arrivals
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: graph coloring

Authors: Hirotaka Yoneda, Masataka Yoneda

We study online graph coloring in the random-arrival model, where the vertices are presented in a uniformly random order. Assuming $n$ and $k$ are known in advance, we present a randomized exponential-time algorithm that colors any $k$-colorable graph on $n$ vertices with $O(k^3 \log^2 k \log^4 n)$ colors in expectation. This is the first online coloring algorithm that uses a polylogarithmic number of colors for all fixed $k \geq 3$, and is better than a known lower bound of $Ω(\log^{k-1} n)$ colors under adversarial arrivals for all fixed $k \geq 6$. In addition, assuming $n$ is known in advance, we obtain a competitive ratio of $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$. For comparison, it is known to be NP-hard to approximate (offline) graph coloring within a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for all fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. Therefore, our exponential-time online algorithm achieves a performance guarantee beyond the NP-hardness threshold for polynomial-time approximation algorithms.

item.title: Constructive Arithmetic Regularity for Abelian Groups
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Swarnalipa Datta, Arijit Ghosh, Chandrima Kayal, Manmatha Roy

The arithmetic regularity lemma of Green is a fundamental tool in additive combinatorics, providing a decomposition of arbitrary subsets of finite Abelian groups into pseudorandom pieces with respect to Fourier analysis. Over the years, it has found numerous applications in combinatorics, property testing, and theoretical computer science. However, Green's proof is existential, and many algorithmic applications require an efficient procedure for constructing the underlying regular decomposition. De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio (SODA 2022) developed a query-efficient constructive regularity framework over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and explicitly raised the problem of extending their dimension-independent sumset-estimation algorithm to other finite Abelian groups. In this work, we resolve this question for finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. We develop the first constructive version of Green's {\em Arithmetic Regularity Lemma} in this general setting. Given oracle access to a subset of the group, our algorithm computes an implicit description of a regular decomposition together with an oracle representation of a structured subset satisfying the guarantees of Green's lemma. The algorithm runs in time and query complexity polynomial in the regularity parameters and the tower bound, while remaining independent of the size of the ambient group. As applications, we obtain efficient algorithms for removing linear configurations and approximately counting linear images, including weighted sumsets and suitable matrix systems of Cauchy--Schwarz complexity one, over finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. Our results provide a unified algorithmic framework extending dimension-independent constructive arithmetic regularity and its applications beyond $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

item.title: Constant-Factor Local Approximation for Bipartite Densest Subgraph
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local algorithm

Authors: Michael Kapralov, Jakub Łącki, Silvio Lattanzi, Guy Weissenberg

Given a vertex $v$ in a large bipartite graph $G$, can one quickly find a small densely connected region near $v$? This is the algorithmic core of many fraud detection, community detection, and recommender systems. One would like a local algorithm, i.e., an algorithm that probes $G$ in only a small number of locations to find such a region. Our main contribution is the first constant-factor local approximation, independent of the maximum degree of the graph, for the classical notion of bipartite density: if the sides of a bipartite subgraph are $S$ and $T$, its density is $d(S,T):=e(S,T)/\sqrt{|S||T|}$, where $e(S,T)$ is the number of edges between $S$ and $T$. We consider cohesive dense subgraphs, since every dense subgraph contains a cohesive core of at least the same density. For such a cohesive dense subgraph $S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T$ with at most $k$ vertices per side, our algorithm, starting from any vertex in $S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T$, uses $O_ε(k^{4+ε})$ neighbor queries to find a subgraph $X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y$ of density $Ω_ε(d(S,T))$ on $O_ε(k^{2+ε})$ vertices, for every fixed $ε>0$. Our result improves upon the result of Andersen (2010), whose approximation guarantee depends logarithmically on the maximum degree. We complement our positive result with information-theoretic and computational limitations showing that the quadratic dependence on $k$ in the output size is essentially unavoidable for constant-factor approximation. Our main technical innovation is an adaptation of the Lovász-Simonovits curve to the bipartite density problem, based on weak-$\ell_p$ norm bounds.

item.title: No Escape from the Quadratic Barrier: Adaptive Attacks on Linear $\ell_2$ Sketches
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: linear sketch

Authors: Edith Cohen, Uri Stemmer

Linear sketches estimate properties of high-dimensional inputs from a fixed low-dimensional projection. At constant accuracy, randomized Euclidean-norm sketches, notably the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, support exponentially many nonadaptive queries in sketch dimension $k$. For adaptive black-box queries, known privacy-based defenses guarantee $\widetildeΩ(k^2)$ and it remained open whether stronger guarantees were possible. Prior attacks used more queries, restricted the responder, or provided weaker failure guarantees. We show that the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors, even with a computationally unbounded responder that knows the matrix, attack algorithm, history, and query distributions and may change its randomized rule after every query. For every fixed hidden $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ with $n>40k$ and target accuracy $α\in (0,1]$, our black-box attack uses $O(k+α^2k^2\log(2+α^2k))$ queries in $\widetilde{O}(1+α^2k)$ adaptive rounds to force, with constant probability, a round in which a constant fraction of answers have $Ω(α)$ relative error. Our results clarify the limits of defending a fixed compressive linear representation by adapting the prediction rule.

item.title: Improved Space Bounds for Promise Graph Coloring in Adversarial Streams
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: dynamic stream

Authors: Sergio Thoumi

We study promise graph coloring in one pass insertion-only adversarial streams. We give a randomized algorithm that distinguishes 3-colorable graphs from graphs that are not 6-colorable using $O(n^{3/2}\log(n/\varepsilon)\log n)$ bits of space. This provides a truly subquadratic space algorithm for a constant coloring gap, answering an open problem posed by Assadi, Sundaresan, and Yazdanyar [SODA 2026] for $q=3$. Combining this algorithm with the vertex-sampling lemma of Assadi et al.\ yields, for any $144\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\le Q\le n$, a one-pass decision algorithm distinguishing $3$-colorable graphs from graphs that are not $Q$-colorable using $O((n/Q)^{3/2}\log^5 n)$ bits of space. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}((n/Q)^2)$ bound achievable via dynamic streaming techniques. Setting $Q=\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil$ yields a semi-streaming decision algorithm, answering the decision version of another open problem posed by Assadi et al. On the negative side, we prove that distinguishing $χ(G)\le q$ from $χ(G)\ge(q-1)^2$ requires $Ω(n^2/q^5)$ bits of space, improving upon the previously established $q^2/4$ threshold using the same space complexity.

item.title:
TR26-264 | On Testing Finite Groups |
Nader Bshouty
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Let $G=[n]$ and let an unknown binary operation $*:G\times G\to G$ be given by oracle access to its multiplication table. The tester is given $n$ explicitly as part of its input. A query chooses $x,y\in G$ and receives $x*y$. We study randomized adaptive two-sided property testers for deciding whether $(G,*)$ is a group. An input is considered far from the property if one must change at least an $\epsilon$-fraction of the $n^2$ table entries in order to obtain any group operation on the same labeled set. We prove three results. First, there is a tester using $$O\left(n+\frac1\epsilon\right)$$ queries and $\tilde O\left(n+1/\epsilon\right)$ time. In fact, this tester has one-sided error. This improve the Goldreich-Tauber tester~\cite{GoldreichTauber25}, that uses $\tilde O(n/\epsilon)$ queries. Second, if computational efficiency is ignored, a dictionary-and-locator construction combined with an action-consistency test on an expanding Cayley graph gives a tester using $$\tilde O\left(\sqrt{\frac n\epsilon}+\frac1\epsilon\right)$$ queries. This is the first query complexity bound for this problem that is sublinear in $n$. Third, there are infinitely many values of $n$ for which every adaptive randomized two-sided tester needs $$\Omega \left(n^{1/5}+\frac1\epsilon\right)$$ queries. This improves on the $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound of Goldreich and Tauber. The lower bound uses two randomly relabeled abelian groups of almost equal orders, embeds them into multiplication tables on the same $n$-element set, and couples arbitrary adaptive query transcripts.

item.title:
TR26-265 | Near-Optimal Bounds for Testing Residual-String Equality and Parenthesis Languages |
Hadar Strauss
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Residual-String Equality, denoted $\text{ResStringEq}$, is the property consisting of all pairs of strings over $\{0,1,*\}$ that are equal after deleting all `$*$' symbols from them. This property was first introduced by Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya (SODA 2018), who used it to show a lower bound on testing the $\text{Dyck}$ languages, where $\text{Dyck}_m$ is the language consisting of balanced sequences of parentheses over $m$ parenthesis types. They showed that testing $\text{ResStringEq}$ on inputs of length $n$ requires $\Omega(n^{1/5})$ queries, and presented a reduction from testing $\text{ResStringEq}$ to testing $\text{Dyck}_m$ for any $m \geq 2$. Furthermore, they showed that $\text{Dyck}_m$ can be tested with $O(n^{2/5+\delta})$ queries for every constant proximity parameter, where $\delta>0$ is an arbitrarily small constant. In this work, we nearly close the gap, by showing that testing $\text{ResStringEq}$, and hence $\text{Dyck}_m$ (for any $m\geq 2$), requires $\Omega(n^{2/5})$ queries. We also show a stronger lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for testers that make non-adaptive queries. We establish that the $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ bound is nearly tight, by presenting a non-adaptive tester for $\text{ResStringEq}$ that uses $O(n^{1/2+\delta})$ queries for an arbitrarily small constant $\delta>0$. Furthermore, we extend this non-adaptive tester to the $\text{Dyck}$ languages, with the same query complexity. Finally, we improve the dependence on the proximity parameter $\epsilon$ in the tester of Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya, reducing it from $O(1/\epsilon)^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\delta)}$ to $O(1/\epsilon)^{O(\log(1/\delta))}$.

item.title: Optimal Algorithms and Hardness for Max-Cut in Bounded Degree Graphs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: max-cut

Authors: Rares-Darius Buhai, Suprovat Ghoshal, Pravesh Kothari, Euiwoong Lee, Konstantin Makarychev, Yury Makarychev

We give a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $α_{GW} + \tildeΩ(1/d)$-approximation for Max 2-LIN(2) in weighted instances where each vertex appears in at most $d$ constraints. This improves on the $α_{GW}+\tildeΩ(1/d^2)$-approximation guarantee of [Hsieh-Kothari, ICALP'23]. We also show a matching Unique Games hardness under randomized polynomial-time reductions, thereby proving that the gain on $α_{GW}$ is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors. Here, $α_{GW} \approx 0.878$ is the approximation ratio of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm. Our results resolve an open question due to Raghavendra and refute his conjectured optimal approximation ratio of $α_{GW} + \tildeΩ(1/\sqrt{d})$. Our local improvement scheme can be thought of as using an adaptive (based on the neighbors) shift applied to the Gaussian before using the GW sign rounding. This allows us to implement a ``soft but simultaneous'' flipping decision at each vertex as opposed to hard but sequential flipping decisions in prior works. Our hardness results are based on a new sparsification lemma for graphs produced by the reduction from Unique Games [Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, SICOMP'07] that preserves the optimal values up to a factor of $1 \pm ε$ while subsampling to an average degree of only $\tilde{O}(1/ε)$. This is the first example of a CSP in which the optimal advantage on degree-$d$ instances is asymptotically smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ [Trevisan, STOC'01]. A key idea in the proof of our sparsification theorem establishes new bounds on the number of ``nearly optimal'' cuts in the output of the KKMO reduction. This step, in turn, relies on a new, robust inverse Majority-Is-Stablest theorem.

item.title: A 2/3-Approximation Algorithm for the Residual Maximum Matching Problem in General Graphs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: maximum matching

Authors: Quanlong Niu, Riheng Jia

The residual maximum matching problem asks for a maximum matching whose deletion leaves a graph with the largest possible matching number. For unweighted graphs, previous work provides a $1/2$-approximation guarantee in general graphs and a $2/3$ guarantee in graphs with a perfect matching. We present a $2/3$-approximation algorithm running in $O(n^5)$ time, extending the latter guarantee to general graphs. The algorithm improves the residual matching number through single-edge exchanges involving free vertices. We prove that, for any maximum matching that admits no further improvement by such exchanges, the residual matching number is at least $2/3$ of the optimum, and we give an example showing that this bound is tight.
